01 — INTRODUCTION

About me

I'm a third-year Civil Engineering student. My structural coursework, especially Design of Reinforced Concrete Structures, has shaped how I approach a drawing: I want it to be accurate enough to actually build from, not just to look finished.

Day to day, that means AutoCAD for 2D documentation and Autodesk Revit for 3D BIM work, covering everything from early massing through to construction-ready detailing. Everything below comes from coursework or practice I've done on my own.

FEATURED PROJECT

Structural Framing & Foundation Design

A G+5 structural building, detailed as a complete framing package. It starts with pile-supported isolated footings and a full RCC column grid, runs through first-floor beam framing, and ends with reinforcement detailing and a derived bar bending schedule. I built it to practice the full chain of structural documentation, from a foundation layout plan to a steel quantity you could actually order.

FIG 01

Foundation Layout Plan

Grid-referenced foundation plan (1–5, A–F) on M25 grade concrete, tagging each column size (C1/C2/C3) against its footing type and dimensions (F1, F2, F3).

FIG 02

Column Layout Plan

First-floor column layout on a 5000mm x 3000mm structural grid, with local beam-depth callouts (225mm, 150mm) marking level changes across the frame.

FIG 03

First Floor Beam Layout

First floor beam framing plan (FFB – 300 x 600mm) spanning the full column grid, with the staircase opening and north point located.

FIG 04

Column-Footing Detail

Enlarged detail of a typical column-to-footing connection (C2 300x300 on F1 2000x2000), dimensioning pedestal offsets and footing edge distances.

FIG 05

General Arrangement Sheet

A composed drawing sheet (A101) bringing the foundation, column and beam layouts together with a typical footing detail and a full title block — formatted for issue.

FIG 06

3D Structural Model — Pile Foundation

The full G+5 structural frame modeled in 3D on a piled foundation system, showing the column grid, floor slabs and internal staircases carried up through every level.

FIG 07

Reinforcement Detailing

Rebar layout for an isolated footing, column and connecting beam — main and distribution bars, stirrup spacing, and lap/anchorage at the column-footing junction — prepared as the basis for the bar bending schedule below.

02 — SELECTED WORK

Projects

PROJECT 01

Residential Bungalow — 3D Model

A contemporary single-family bungalow modeled in Revit. I used it to study massing and material contrast: a mixed brick-and-render facade, a cantilevered first-floor volume, a pergola entrance and a boundary gate all sit together on one elevation.

PROJECT 02

Bungalow — Elevation & Terrace Render

A rendered corner view of the same house. It's the best angle to see the cantilevered rooftop terrace with its glass balustrade, along with the textured wall panels and covered entrance porch below.

PROJECT 03

Office Layout — Floor Plan

A 2D AutoCAD floor plan for a small office fit-out, laid out on a coordinated column grid (1–5, A–D). It fits three private offices, an officer's cabin, a central passage and dual staircases into the plate.

PROJECT 04

Residential Apartment — Massing Model

A seven-storey apartment block modeled in Revit. I repeated one floor plate straight up the building, added a perimeter balcony railing and a rooftop service block, and used it mainly to get comfortable keeping a facade rhythm consistent over many floors.

PROJECT 05

Staircase & Ramp Families

Three Revit families built for practice: an L-shaped stair with a mid-landing, a long straight-run stair, and an accessible ramp with continuous handrails. Each one has properly modeled stringers, treads and guardrails, not just a placeholder mass.

PROJECT 06

Wall & Level Study — Two-Storey Volume

A cutaway massing study, mainly an exercise in setting up levels correctly: a 900mm plinth at Ground Floor, a 4500mm floor-to-floor height above it, with window and door openings cut into an internal room layout.

PROJECT 07

Roof Types — Practice Sheet

Nine roof forms modeled side by side on the same simple footprint, just to see how each Revit roof tool actually behaves: gable, hip, pyramid hip, a gambrel with a dormer, half-hip, shed, barrel and butterfly.

PROJECT 08

Residential Floor Plan — Flooring Layout

A detailed floor plan built around flooring, not just walls: room-by-room tile patterns, door swings, and dimension strings at 3500mm and 3900mm bays, all coordinated with an attached garage footprint.

03 — SOFTWARE

Core features of Revit

Building Information Modeling (BIM)

Every wall, door and slab is a real 3D object carrying its own data, not just lines — so the model, plans, sections and elevations all update together automatically.

Parametric Families

Components like doors, windows and stairs are built as flexible "families" whose size, style and material can be adjusted with parameters, rather than redrawn each time.

Automatic Scheduling

Quantity take-offs — door counts, wall areas, material volumes — are generated straight from the model as live schedules, so drawings and quantities never fall out of sync.

Worksharing

Multiple people can work inside the same central model at once, each editing separate elements, which mirrors how a real design team collaborates on a project.

Phasing & Design Options

Existing, demolished and new construction can be modeled on separate phases, and multiple design alternatives can be studied within one project file before a final choice is made.

Clash Detection

Structural, architectural and MEP models can be checked against each other to flag physical clashes — a duct running through a beam, for instance — before construction starts.

Detailing & Annotation

Dimensions, tags, keynotes and construction details are linked to the model, so a change to the building updates every annotated drawing that references it.

Rendering & Visualization

Materials, lighting and cameras built into the model produce photorealistic renders and walkthroughs directly, without rebuilding the geometry in a separate program.
